lead: Durham plumbing deals with red clay, old mill-era houses, big trees and crawl spaces. PipeMend sends licensed local plumbers across Durham.
risk: tree roots in old sewer lines, aging pipes in older homes and frozen crawl-space pipes
risk_short: sewer roots, old pipes and frozen pipes
why: Trinity Park, Walltown and Old West Durham have homes from the early 1900s, many with galvanized supply lines and clay sewer laterals. Mature trees send roots into those old lines.
Many homes sit on crawl spaces, and ice storms freeze exposed pipes. Homes from the 1980s and early 1990s may have polybutylene pipe.
utility: City of Durham Department of Water Management
water: Durham draws its water mainly from Lake Michie and the Little River Reservoir. The water is relatively soft.
problems: Trinity Park, Walltown and older areas
tips: Scope the sewer line before buying an older home.
Plant trees away from the sewer line.
areas: PipeMend works in Downtown, Trinity Park, Walltown, Old West Durham, Forest Hills, Hope Valley and every other Durham neighborhood.
permits: Plumbing permits come from the Durham City-County Inspections Department, and plumbing contractors must be licensed by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Plumbing, Heating and Fire Sprinkler Contractors.

faq.q: Who issues plumbing permits in Durham?
faq.a: The Durham City-County Inspections Department issues permits for both the city and the county. Your plumber usually pulls the permit and books the inspection.
